subject: linear-algebra
title: Quadratic forms
introduction: A quadratic form $x^TAx$ measures curvature and signed energy. Symmetry lets you read its behavior from eigenvalues or principal minors instead of testing infinitely many vectors.
theory: Only the symmetric part of a matrix affects $x^TAx$. Positive definiteness means the form is positive for every nonzero vector; semidefiniteness allows zero directions.
For real symmetric matrices, definiteness is determined by eigenvalue signs. Sylvester’s criterion uses leading principal minors for positive definiteness.

examples.title: Two-variable form
examples.solution: $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&2\\2&3\end{bmatrix}$. Leading minors are 2 and 2, so $A$ is positive definite.

examples.title: Indefinite
examples.solution: $q(1,0)=2>0$ and $q(0,1)=-1<0$, so the form is indefinite.

examples.title: Skew part vanishes
examples.solution: $x^TKx=-(x^TKx)^T$, so the scalar equals its negative and must be zero.

examples.title: Optimization link
examples.problem: A twice differentiable function has positive-definite Hessian at a stationary point.
examples.solution: The point is a strict local minimum.

pitfalls: Applying Sylvester’s criterion to a nonsymmetric representation without symmetrizing.
Calling a matrix positive definite because diagonal entries are positive.
Treating positive semidefinite as strictly positive.
Forgetting the factor of two in off-diagonal terms such as $2a_{12}xy$.
whyGate: Quadratic forms encode loss curvature, covariance geometry, regularization, and second-order optimality.
